source: Verma (2026) Try Again, Don't Look Back: Blind Resampling Outperforms Self-Repair in Small Code Models
finding: Placebo-controlled test of what a failed attempt in context does. Showing a small model its own failed program made it less likely to succeed than simply resampling from the original prompt. Real execution feedback added nothing over a content-free 'wrong' notice. Authors name the mechanism anchoring: the model edits instead of rethinking.
numbers: MBPP+ 378 tasks, Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B/3B/7B, k=8 retries, pre-registered, McNemar + Holm. pass@1: 1.5B resample 0.749 vs placebo 0.688 (-0.061, p=0.006); 3B 0.778 vs 0.709 (-0.069, p<0.001); 7B 0.820 vs 0.802 (tie). Feedback minus placebo +0.000/+0.026/+0.008, none significant. Similarity between consecutive attempts +0.30 to +0.38; near-identical retries (>0.95) 33-68% vs 2-14%. Retrieved solutions to OTHER tasks changed pass@1 by at most 3.5 points. Replicates on DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B and at full precision; penalty size predicted by baseline quality (r=0.96). Blind resampling used 2.5-5.5x fewer tokens. Reflection weakened the anchor (similarity -0.04 to -0.12 vs feedback) but cost 2.5x tokens for +0.8 points at 7B (n.s.).
quote: Conditioning on the model's failed attempt costs 6.1 points at 1.5B (p=0.006)
limits: Small open models only (1.5B-7B), single-function MBPP+, single-author preprint. Penalty shrinks with model strength, so it may be near zero for frontier models. Placebo vs feedback ranking does not follow the similarity measure.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a failed attempt left in context acts as an anchor, and that the harm is self-conditioning, not long context. Supports a clean-context retry rule for G3 on weak models; says little yet about frontier models.

source: Arimbur (2026) How Many Tries Does It Take? Iterative Self-Repair in LLM Code Generation Across Model Scales and Benchmarks
finding: Opposite pattern for modern, larger instruction-tuned models: self-repair with error feedback beats or matches independent resampling for all but the smallest model, and uses fewer tokens.
numbers: HumanEval 164, MBPP-Sanitized 257, 7 models, up to 5 attempts. Self-repair gain +4.9 to +17.1 pp (HumanEval), +16.0 to +30.0 pp (MBPP). HumanEval self-repair (greedy, 5 rounds) vs resampling pass@5 (T=0.8): Llama 3.1 8B 76.8 vs 79.9; Llama 3.3 70B 93.3 vs 90.9; Llama 4 Scout 89.6 vs 86.0; Qwen3 32B 92.7 vs 92.7. Self-repair tokens 11% (8B) to 54% (Qwen3) fewer. Most gain in first two rounds. Assertion (logic) errors hardest: about 45% repaired. Gemini 2.5 Pro (90.2) below Flash (96.3) on HumanEval.
limits: Not a clean test: repair is greedy, resampling is T=0.8, so decoding differs; no placebo notice arm; resampling done on 4 models only. Repair keeps the failed code in context, so it shows feedback helps at scale but does not isolate anchoring cost.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence to d01: the failed-attempt penalty fades for models of 30B+ with real test feedback. A fresh-context retry is not clearly better for strong models.

source: Jha (2026) Does Fault Localization Beat a Fresh Attempt? A Placebo-Controlled Study of Test-Guided Code Repair
finding: Third independent placebo-style study: focusing the repair on the suspect span loses to a blind whole-solution resample from scratch, because span infilling reproduces the removed code.
numbers: 3 frozen 26-32B models, 3 benchmarks, 488 failing candidates; only 9.0% of failures expose a usable failing public test. Among 177 localizable candidates, localized infilling vs blind resampling 3:40 (p=3.0e-9). Mistral-Small-24B replication: 0.6% vs 11.9% (-11.3 pts, 95% CI [-16.6,-6.8]). Span infilling reproduces the removed span verbatim in 48.9% of attempts; 0.23 distinct programs per attempt vs 0.83 for blind. 21.7 vs 371.1 generated tokens per attempt, but 16 localized attempts reach 6.8% while one blind attempt reaches 10.1%.
limits: Single-author preprint, models 24-32B, three benchmarks of function-level tasks. Measures edit locality, not in-context failed text directly.
agent_relevance: Same direction as d01 at 26-32B: staying close to the failed candidate wastes attempts. Diversity of attempts matters; log whether retries are near-copies.

source: Yang (2026) Why Retrying Fails: Context Contamination in LLM Agent Pipelines
finding: A formal model (CCRM) where after one failed attempt the per-step error rate rises. Proves restarting with cleared context needs fewer attempts. The only data check is a fit to a public SWE-bench Verified pass@1/pass@3 report.
numbers: Fit to a vendor report: pass@1 76.1%, pass@3 81.2%. An independent-attempt model predicts pass@3 98.6% (17.4 points too high). The contamination model fits with error <0.001, implying a cascade ratio of 7.1 (p0=0.761, p1=0.113). Monte Carlo n=30,000 matches the theory.
limits: p1 is inferred from two aggregate numbers (one data point fits two parameters), not measured from retries with and without failed context. Task heterogeneity (hard tasks fail every time) also lowers pass@3 gaps, so the same fit has a rival explanation. Binary contamination assumed. Theory, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Do not cite as evidence. It gives a vocabulary and a budget formula only.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models (retry experiment, section 7.2)
finding: Models told 'your previous answer was incorrect, review your reasoning and try again' (history kept, up to 5 retries) on AIME 2025 and Beyond AIME. Qwen3-8B fine-tuned on Wason-task falsification traces solved more than the base model. This is a retry-with-failure-in-context setup, but no clean-context arm was run.
numbers: Qwen3-8B base vs Wason-distilled: AIME 2025 0.33 vs 0.60 (McNemar p=0.0386); Beyond AIME 0.30 vs 0.40 (p=0.0414). Qwen3-32B: 0.73 vs 0.80 (p=0.6875) and 0.52 vs 0.54 (p=0.7539), n.s. GSM8K accuracy of distilled models within 2% of base (8B small drop).
limits: Math, not code. Limitations section says real-world tasks such as debugging were not tested. Small item counts (AIME has 30 problems). Gain is from training, not from a prompt.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 check: falsification training transfers to math self-correction on a small model; transfer to code repair is untested. Retrying with history is common practice and was not compared with a fresh start.

source: Haeri and Ghelichi (2026) Specification Grounding Drives Test Effectiveness for LLM Code
finding: Controlled test-writer study on Python tasks, frontier models. Changing one line so the test writer gets the spec as a checklist of rules raises final correct code by about 38 points over an already edge-prompted baseline. In every arm, expected outputs come from the ticket or rules, never from the candidate code, so this does not compare code-visible vs code-hidden.
numbers: 26 bespoke Python tasks (18 specification-completeness, 8 logic), Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.8. 8 core tasks: ONESHOT 38%, FREE 38% (0/30 bugs caught), FREE2K 42%, FREE+ 60% (18/30), SPEC 100% (30/30). Three model sizes: 62% vs 100% (+38 pp). Held-out 4 tasks: 25% vs 61% (+36). Scale-up 6 tasks: 78% vs 96% (+18). GPT-5.3-codex 72% to 100% (+28); Gemini 3.5 Flash 72% to 92% (+19). Task-level sign test over 18 tasks p=0.002 (core 8 alone p=0.06). Spec as plain paragraph: tester recovers 27/30 bugs; no spec 2/30. False alarms on correct code 0% (SPEC) vs 33% (FREE+), up to 68% vs stdlib oracle. Real-library slice: 90% vs 40% (+50 pp).
limits: Author-written small pure functions, mostly missing-validation bugs; the 8 logic tasks and HumanEval+ (5 model families) show no gap. Needs a human or model written spec. Authors flag test-author strength as a limit. Preprint from one team.
agent_relevance: Strong support, on a non-Java benchmark and frontier models, that tests anchored to the stated rules beat tests that probe 'edge cases' freely. Agent rule: S1 writes the rules, S4 turns each rule into one check. Good for G3 but only helps where the bug is an unstated edge.

source: Haeri and Ghelichi (2026) Specification Grounding (imperfect-spec, scope and HumanEval+ checks)
finding: Tests how the method fails when the spec is wrong or incomplete. Dropping validation rules lowers detection but tests stay accurate; a wrong rule that endorses the bug does not hide the bug but lowers test precision. On well-specified algorithmic benchmark HumanEval+ the gap vanishes.
numbers: Five buggy core tasks. Incomplete spec: detection 30/30 -> 6/30, tester accuracy stays 100%. Noisy spec (wrong rule endorsing the bug): detection stays 30/30 because the correct rule's test still fires, tester accuracy falls to 82.8% (15 of 87 tests disagree with truth). Rules the model derives itself from the ticket recover only part of the benefit (restate happy path). HumanEval+ under EvalPlus oracle, five model families: gap vanishes.
limits: Same single study. 'Spec inherits the bug' share was not measured as a rate; it was injected on purpose.
agent_relevance: Answers part of gap 2: a spec that endorses the bug lowers precision rather than hiding the bug when the correct rule is also present. When the bug is the only source of the rule, the wrong rule would win. Keep the agent's own derived rules suspect.

source: Ma and Eisty (2026) From Business Requirements to Test Assertions: Evaluating LLM-Generated Oracles on Real Bugs
finding: Pilot: five LLMs write Java test oracles from a natural-language requirement only, with no source code or diff. Oracles agree more with the requirement-derived gold oracle than with the (buggy) system under test for four of five models.
numbers: Defects4J Lang, 10 bugs (1, 3-11), DeepSeek-V3, Gemma-3n, Llama-3, Mistral-7B, Qwen-3. Macro-F1 vs requirement oracle / vs SUT: DeepSeek-V3 0.818 / 0.748; Llama-3 0.780 / 0.714; Qwen-3 0.778 / 0.703; Gemma-3n 0.595 / 0.636; Mistral-7B 0.560 / 0.543. Requirement-based gold oracle vs SUT macro-F1 0.793. Requirement technicality or ambiguity vs accuracy: weak correlation, wide CI. Bug 8 easy (perfect); bug 10 range 0.40-0.85.
limits: Ten bugs, one Java project, requirements written by hand from the fix diff (so they encode the fix), no code-visible comparison arm, no frontier closed model. Authors call it a pilot.
agent_relevance: Weak support only: spec-only generation works, with high variance. Does not answer whether code-visible tests are worse. Gap 2 stays open on that comparison.

source: Salman, Turhan and Vegas (2019) A controlled experiment on time pressure and confirmation bias in functional software testing
finding: Independent human replication of the positive-test finding in software testing. Graduate students wrote far more specification-consistent (confirmatory) test cases than inconsistent ones. Time pressure did not raise the confirmatory rate. The paper also argues earlier studies (Leventhal, Teasley) may have labelled tests differently.
numbers: 42 graduate students, 21 per group (30 min under time pressure vs 60 min without). 371 usable test cases: consistent 150+171=321 (86.5%), inconsistent 24+26=50. Overall confirmatory > disconfirmatory: p=2.2e-8, r=0.598 (large). Mean confirmation score z TP 0.374, NTP 0.428. Time-pressure effect: d=-0.357, p=0.87 (n.s., wrong direction). Over 80% of participants had under 6 months of testing experience. Marking agreement 66%; 14 of 385 test cases dropped.
limits: One system (MusicFone) with a spec closer to 'positive only'; students, little experience; no code under test shown at design time; consistent test was defined by conformity to the spec, so with a complete spec a confirmatory test is not bad. Authors ask for replications of the time-pressure part.
agent_relevance: Confirms that people write mostly spec-fitting tests even without time pressure, so 'be careful' is not enough; an explicit falsification step is needed. Also warns that G3 needs a definition of 'tests that could fail' tied to the spec.

source: Leventhal, Teasley and Rohlman (1994) Analyses of factors related to positive test bias in software testing (Int. J. Human-Computer Studies 41(5), 717-749)
finding: Two studies. Study 1 varied tester expertise, spec completeness and whether the program had errors; positive test bias showed up in every condition and was partly reduced by more expertise and more complete specs. Study 2 (think-aloud) found the spec drives the hypotheses testers form.
numbers: Not recorded: only abstract text from a search result was seen. Full text blocked. Exact cell sizes and percentages unknown.
limits: Not opened. Salman 2019 (d09) says the study classified tests as valid or invalid equivalence classes, a different labelling than spec-consistent, which makes direct number comparison unsafe. No replication with LLM test writers found.
agent_relevance: Weakly supports: more complete specs lower positive bias. Haeri (d06, d07) gives the LLM analogue: tests grounded in complete rules catch far more bugs. The moderator claim for LLMs rests on one preprint.

source: Teasley, Leventhal, Mynatt and Rohlman (1994) Why software testing is sometimes ineffective: two applied studies of positive test strategy (J. Applied Psychology 79(1), 142-155)
finding: Two experiments on tester expertise and functional testing: testers mostly tested only the functions the spec described. Pairs with Leventhal 1994 as the founding software positive-test studies. Another source quoted: testers about four times more likely to pick positive tests.
numbers: Not recorded: abstract-level only, from a search result and from Salman 2019's literature review.
limits: Not opened; numbers second-hand.
agent_relevance: Background for G3 only.

source: Branchini et al. (2025) Thinking in opposites improves hypothesis testing performance in Wason's rule-discovery task (Memory and Cognition)
finding: A randomised human experiment: asking people to list properties of the seed triple and then think of the opposite of each, for use when testing, nearly doubled success. The gain came from less repeated testing of the same hypothesis and more testing of the ascending-descending dimension, not from more tests. Listing properties alone (no opposites) did nothing.
numbers: N=180, randomly assigned, 60 per condition. Correct solution: opposites training 78.33%, properties-only 38.33%, no-prompt control 36.66%; chi2(2, N=180)=27.986, p<.001. Correct rule found earlier in the opposites group than control (F(2,89)=5.702, p=.004). Solution took longer in the two training groups. About 15 min for the task.
quote: Thinking in opposites nearly doubled the success rate
limits: Students on a 2-4-6 task, three attempts, no software. Prompt-style training, no delayed test and no transfer test. This is the human original of the TiO prompt used in d05 and in claim K02.
agent_relevance: This is the only randomised human trial found where a short instruction raises disconfirmatory testing. It is not software training. Supports a one-line falsification prompt in the agent, but its transfer to code is untested.

source: Sellier, Scopelliti and Morewedge (2019) Debiasing Training Improves Decision Making in the Field (Psychological Science 30(9))
finding: A one-shot game-based training for confirmation bias transferred to an unannounced business case. Assignment was by natural variation in the training schedule, not random. Trained students were less likely to choose the inferior hypothesis-confirming option.
numbers: N=290 graduate students after 26 exclusions (316 tested; 217 MBA, 64 MS entrepreneurship, 35 MS strategy). Trained n=182, untrained n=108. Chose the confirming solution: trained 58.8% vs untrained 72.2% (Wald chi2(1)=5.23, p=.022, odds 0.549); 29% relative reduction. Game 80-100 min, three episodes, includes Wason 2-4-6-style, Tschirgi and Snyder-Swann hypothesis-testing paradigms.
limits: Quasi-experimental (timing of training), business case not software, one case, no delayed outcome. Not a software trial. 'Training' here is game plus feedback.
agent_relevance: Non-software evidence that logic or hypothesis-testing training can lower confirmatory choices in the field; supports the human-side claim only by analogy. For a model, the analogue is an in-context prompt, not training.

source: Calikli and Bener (2010) Empirical analyses of the factors affecting confirmation bias and the effects of confirmation bias on software developer/tester performance (PROMISE 2010); Calikli and Bener (2015) Software Quality Journal 23(4):695-722
finding: Resolves the Mohanani P4 question: the PROMISE 2010 paper is the companion to the PPIG paper. Per the repository abstract it measures confirmation bias with pen-and-paper and interactive tests built on two cognitive-psychology tasks, reports a direct correlation between confirmation bias and defect proneness of code, and says logical reasoning and hypothesis-testing skills separate low-bias people. The 2015 journal article tests factors such as methodology (incremental, agile, TDD), company size and education level.
numbers: Not recorded: only repository abstract text seen. Full PDFs of PROMISE 2010, PPIG 2010, the 2013 paper (defect link on five datasets from two companies) and the 2015 paper blocked (HTTP 403 or bot check).
limits: Not opened. Same research group for all versions: not independent replications. No external replication of the logic-training claim found, and no randomised trial in software testers found.
agent_relevance: Does not change K14 or K15: the human logic-to-bias link stays one research group's correlational work.

source: Borjigin, Hermann, Cyron and Aydin (2026) AnchorBench: A Multi-Pathway Benchmark for the Anchoring Effect in LLMs (COLM 2026)
finding: Anchoring in LLMs depends on how the anchor arrives (external, history, RAG, tool, in-context example). Plausible anchors move answers more than irrelevant ones through strong pathways. High anchor-free accuracy does not protect: frontier API models above 95% control accuracy are still moved by plausible anchors, though less than open models.
numbers: 14 instruction-tuned models (10 open-weight, 4 API incl. Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5.4-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash). Anchor-pathway table (Claude-H4.5): external 0.71, history 0.00, RAG 0.29, tool 0.03, ICL 0.00; Gemini-2.5-Flash 0.79, 0.23, 0.47, 0.33, 0.00; Gemma-4B 0.38, 0.00, 1.03, 0.29, 0.00 (column labels read from a garbled table; treat as approximate). Influence weakens as the anchor moves farther from the evidence.
limits: Numeric rating-aggregation task, not code. Metric is a normalised anchoring index. Answer-only protocol. No reasoning-model arm in the main panel.
agent_relevance: Supports treating any in-context number, estimate or earlier answer as a possible anchor and checking the pathway. Pathway matters: the history pathway was near zero for Claude Haiku 4.5 here.

source: Borjigin et al. (2026) AnchorBench, appendix A.17.7 chain-of-thought vs answer-only
finding: Letting the model reason first lowers plausible-anchor influence in most cells but rarely removes it and sometimes raises it. This is a controlled check on whether reasoning helps on one probe set.
numbers: 5-model panel x 3 suites (External, RAG, History) = 15 cells. CoT lowers plausible-anchor influence (UAIpls) in 11 of 15 cells (mean change -0.06); lowers both plausible and irrelevant influence in only 6 cells; raises plausible-anchor influence in 4. UAIpls still above 0 under CoT in 13 of 15 cells. One cell repeated across runs differed by 0.02 even with byte-identical prompts.
limits: Chain-of-thought text on non-reasoning models, not a native reasoning model with thinking toggled. Numeric rating task. Open-weight panel plus one API model.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 5: on one common probe set, thinking helps a little, inconsistently. Consistent with Kraishan's null (K10). Second-hand: AnchorBench cites Takenami et al. 2025 that reasoning models are less susceptible in multi-turn price negotiation (not opened).

source: Borjigin et al. (2026) AnchorBench, appendix A.17.8 task specification: rule vs judgment
finding: Telling the model the exact rule ('your estimate should be the unweighted arithmetic mean of the visible ratings') removes most of the measured anchoring. A vague 'weight sources by credibility' instruction does not.
numbers: External pathway, open-weight panel. Plausible-anchor index (UAIpls) mean: baseline 0.33, +Rule 0.06, +Judgment 0.26. Irrelevant-anchor index: 0.09, 0.01, 0.12. Gemma-4B 0.51 to 0.08 with the rule; Llama-8B 0.32 to 0.01.
quote: A drop from Baseline to +Rule indicates the published anchoring effect is partly driven by task underspecification.
limits: Small open models, numeric aggregation where a rule exists. Shows part of 'anchoring' is task under-specification. Does not hold where no explicit rule exists (open-ended code design).
agent_relevance: Second independent source (with PROBE-SWE axiomatic cues, K12) that writing out the correct rule before answering cuts bias. Agent action at S1: state the rule or criterion the answer must satisfy before looking at anchors.

source: Huang, Zhang, Kwak and An (2026) CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in Large Language Models
finding: Benchmark with four bias families. Prompt-level debiasing helped response-order bias a lot but made judgment biases (base-rate, anchoring, sunk cost, status quo) slightly worse. Activation steering cut bias scores 26-32%.
numbers: 3 models (GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B). Debiasing effect: Judgment accuracy -4.4% (backfires), Information Processing -1.1%, Social +5.9%, Response position independence +40.5%. Steering: bias score down 26-32%; Llama under 1 pp capability loss, Qwen up to 19.0 pp for Judgment biases. Family order of bias was the same in all three models.
limits: Vignette tasks, three mid-size instruction-tuned models, activation access needed for steering. Not code.
agent_relevance: Warns against 'be unbiased' style prompts for anchoring and similar judgment biases. Matches K08 and PROBE-SWE. Steering is outside our scaffold-only scope.

source: Jhang (2026) Multi-Estimate Elicitation Does Not Uniformly Debias Language Model Judgments
finding: Asking for five weighted estimates in one answer, instead of one, does not reliably debias anchoring, hindsight, base-rate, conjunction or default tasks. Only one effect beat the minimum meaningful size. On base-rate integration, direct answers already followed Bayes closely (ceiling).
numbers: 6 frozen configurations (incl. Claude Sonnet 5.5, Qwen3-8B, gpt-oss-120b, Gemini Flash low/high), 22,212 formal units. Of 45 preregistered confirmatory tests across 5 configurations, 12 rejected on complete cases, 11 retained after missingness protection. Largest: gpt-oss-120b +10.68 points more post-outcome confirmation error (worst case 10.04). Base-rate (Experiment C): direct slopes near 1 with small posterior errors; multi-estimate raised posterior error by about 1.006 pp (Sonnet) and 0.647 pp (Qwen3).
limits: Not a test of reference-class or outside-view prompting; it tests answer format. Base-rate items were word problems with given probabilities, not planning forecasts. Ceiling effect limits conclusions. Single author.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: no study found that asks an LLM for a reference-class base rate before it estimates its own success. This paper only shows frontier models already use stated base rates correctly, and that extra estimates do not help. Optimism needs its own measurement.

source: Huang, Pang, Zhang, Cheng and Ma (2026) Does More Thinking Pay Off? Reasoning Cost and Correctness of LLMs in Code Generation and Bug Fixing
finding: Paired reasoning on/off test on code. Turning reasoning on in Qwen3-32B raised pass@1 on some tasks and not others, and a longer trace did not reliably mean higher accuracy. Not a bias measure, but it is the only same-model on-code reasoning toggle in this set.
numbers: 866 Python tasks (HumanEval Pro, MBPP Pro, BugsInPy), 5 model settings, 5 runs. Qwen3-32B HumanEval Pro 71.1% to 76.5%; BugsInPy tests passing 3.5% to 7.9%; MBPP Pro 68.1% to 69.5% (n.s., median over 2,000 thinking tokens). Keeping only the first half of a trace gave no significant correctness drop.
limits: No anchoring or confirmation probe in this paper; context only for gap 5. One model family toggled.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open for bias. Reasoning helps correctness unevenly, so any bias benefit of thinking would need a direct probe on our model with thinking on and off.

source: Impact of Request Formats on Effort Estimation: Are LLMs Different Than Humans? (ACM 2025; replication of human effort-estimation experiments)
finding: Replicates five classic human effort-estimation experiments on LLMs. Switching from 'how much effort for X' to 'how much can be done in Y hours' lowered estimates in the first four experiments, and the fifth and first showed patterns like anchoring on the 'Y work-hours' figure.
numbers: Abstract only (via OpenAlex): GPT-4, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3.1; 88 specifications per treatment per experiment; 880 prompts from 704 user stories (Hyperledger Fabric, Mulesoft Mule, Spring XD). Effect sizes not seen.
limits: Full text blocked; abstract only. Older models. Request wording is the anchor, so it is an estimation-task link, not a stated-confidence probe.
agent_relevance: Closest software-estimation analogue to the Wyrich framing finding (gap 8). Does not test stated confidence vs accuracy. Gap 8 stays open.

source: Gap-search negative results (searches run 2026-11-10, not a paper)
finding: Targeted searches for four items returned no study: (1) a randomised trial of logic or hypothesis-testing training on positive test bias in software testers; (2) a replication of Calikli et al. 2010 by another group; (3) a test of a forced falsification step on real-code fix correctness at matched tokens; (4) a base-vs-instruct comparison on a falsification probe.
numbers: Searches: about 15 OpenAlex queries and 8 web searches. Semantic Scholar and the arXiv API returned HTTP 429 (rate limit) for most calls, so coverage is partial.
limits: Absence of evidence in a rate-limited search is weak. The Branchini RCT (d12) and Sellier quasi-experiment (d13) are the nearest items and neither is in software.
agent_relevance: Treat falsification-step benefit on real code, instruct-vs-base effect and human debiasing in software as open questions in the schema notes.
